tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

skill.description: The name of a skill from the available-skills list. Do not guess names.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

query.description: Query to find deferred tools. Use "select:<tool_name>" for direct selection, or keywords to search.

max_results.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 5)

tools.name: Write
tools.description:
Writes a file to the local filesystem, overwriting if one exists.

When to use: creating a new file, or fully replacing one you've already Read. Overwriting an existing file you haven't Read will fail. For partial changes, use Edit instead.

file_path.description: The absolute path to the file to write (must be absolute, not relative)

content.description: The content to write to the file

tools.name: mcp__claude_ai_Claude_Docs__read
tools.description: Read a doc (lists its tabs), a tab's contents, or a comment. A claude.ai/[code/]artifact/[<title>-]<id> link → `ref {"object":"project","id":"<id>"}` first; reads inside it take `container {"kind":"project","id":"<id>"}`.

tools.name: mcp__plugin_design_notion__notion-create-pages
tools.description:
Creates one or more Notion pages with the specified properties and content.

## Core rules

**IMPORTANT**: Before writing page content, read the MCP resource `notion://docs/notion-flavored-markdown-spec` through your MCP client's resource-reading interface, or call the Notion "fetch" tool with this URI if your client does not support reading MCP resources. Do NOT pass this URI to any other URL-fetching tool. Do NOT guess or hallucinate Markdown syntax. Do not put the page title at the top of content; set it in properties. By default, use native Notion mentions for references you add to existing Notion pages, databases, data sources, people, and dates. Use Markdown links only for external URLs or when the user requests a plain link. For a person, use a user mention with their user URL, found with search using query_type "user"; do not write "@Name" as plain text. For a specific date or time, such as a due date or meeting time, use a date mention. The Markdown specification gives the mention syntax.

Use a named destination as parent. Otherwise use "creation_mode": "draft" for a durable private page. Do not combine draft mode with parent, or move or share it without direction.

For a meeting note, use create_meeting_note if available, even in a Meetings database, unless the user wants a regular page.

For a database destination, ALWAYS fetch first. Use its collection:// URL as data_source_id, exact property names, and title property. Never put a database ID in page_id. Outside a database, the only allowed property is the required "title".

For reusable instructions, set "is_skill": true. Before creating a skill, read the MCP resource `notion://docs/skills` through your MCP client's resource-reading interface. If your client does not support reading MCP resources, call the Notion "fetch" tool with this URI instead. Do NOT pass this URI to any other URL-fetching tool. Do not mark ordinary pages or drafts as skills. Report any "warnings" in the result to the user.

properties.description:
The properties of the new page, which is a JSON map of property names to SQLite values.
For pages in a database, use the SQLite schema definition shown in <database>.
For pages outside of a database, the only allowed property is "title", which is the title of the page and is automatically shown at the top of the page as a large heading.
**IMPORTANT**: Some property types require specific formats:
- Date properties: Split into "date:{property}:start", "date:{property}:end" (optional), and "date:{property}:is_datetime" (0 or 1)
- Place properties: Split into "place:{property}:name", "place:{property}:address", "place:{property}:latitude", "place:{property}:longitude", and "place:{property}:google_place_id" (optional)
- Number properties: Use JavaScript numbers (not strings)
- Checkbox properties: Use "__YES__" for checked, "__NO__" for unchecked
- Relation properties: Use an array of related page URLs or page IDs, e.g. ["https://www.notion.so/[redacted]", "26ab1f9f-4c5f-80b1-8d3b-d10a6b1d2f4e"]
- Person properties: Use an array of user IDs, user or agent URLs, or group references copied from fetch output ("space_permission_group-<UUID>"). Bare group UUIDs are also supported.
- Files properties: Use a JSON array of file IDs, Notion Folder URLs, and/or <folder> tags copied from fetch output. Folders are stored as native Folder references, not ordinary links.


**Special property naming**: Properties named "id" or "url" (case insensitive) must be prefixed with "userDefined:" (e.g., "userDefined:URL", "userDefined:id")

content.description: The content of the new page, using Notion Markdown. For people and dates, use user and date mentions rather than plain text; notion://docs/notion-flavored-markdown-spec gives the syntax.

template_id.description: The ID of a template to apply to this page. When specified, do not provide 'content' as the template will provide it. Properties can still be set alongside the template. Get template IDs from the <templates> section in the fetch tool results. Template application is asynchronous: the page starts blank and content appears shortly after.

icon.description: An emoji character (e.g. "🚀"), a custom emoji by name (e.g. ":rocket_ship:"), a Notion icon identifier as returned by fetch (e.g. "icons/pizza_blue"), or an external image URL. Use "none" to explicitly set no icon. Omit to leave unchanged. Keep the title free of a duplicate leading emoji because the icon renders separately.

cover.description: An external image URL for the page cover. Use "none" to explicitly set no cover. Omit to leave unchanged.

is_skill.description: Set to true only when the user asks for reusable instructions or a repeatable workflow. Do not mark ordinary reference pages, one-time documents, or drafts as skills. Before creating a skill, read the MCP resource `notion://docs/skills` through your MCP client's resource-reading interface. If your client does not support reading MCP resources, call the Notion "fetch" tool with this URI instead. Do NOT pass this URI to any other URL-fetching tool. False has the same effect as omitting the field.

preserve_internal_links.description: Preserve internal Markdown links instead of converting them to native mentions.

creation_mode.description: If the user explicitly names a private or shared destination, omit "creation_mode" and use that parent. Otherwise, use "draft" when the user clearly wants a durable page but has not named a destination. Prefer this explicit draft mode over omitting the parent. Draft mode is server-enforced: it creates a private workspace-level page and cannot be combined with "parent". Create it without first asking where it should live. After creation, tell the user it is private and offer to move it once they name a destination.

parent.description: All pages in one call share this parent. Pass "memory" to save a personal memory; see notion://docs/memory. Otherwise use a page (page_id), database page (database_id), data source (data_source_id), or teamspace root (teamspace_id, from get_teams). Teamspace roots require a user-backed connection and permission to add top-level pages. A database_id cannot be used when the database has more than one data source; fetch it and use the right collection:// URL as data_source_id. If omitted, pages are private at the workspace level. When no destination is named, prefer explicit "creation_mode": "draft" over omitting the parent.

page_id.description: The ID of the parent page (with or without dashes), for example, [redacted]

type.description: Always `page_id`

database_id.description: The ID of the parent database (with or without dashes), for example, [redacted]

type.description: Always `database_id`

data_source_id.description: The ID of the parent data source (collection), with or without dashes. For example, f336d0bc-b841-465b-8045-024475c079dd

type.description: Always `data_source_id`

teamspace_id.description: The ID of the teamspace in which to create top-level pages (with or without dashes).

allow_async.description: Default to true for page creation. Set to false only when the next step needs the created pages immediately, or when async execution rejects the request as too large. When this create operation is accepted for background execution, it returns an async_task result. Use get_async_task to wait for a succeeded status before taking a dependent action on the pages. For pages created with template_id, a succeeded status does not mean template content is ready; fetch and retry until it is ready before changing or relying on that content. If omitted or false, the tool keeps the existing synchronous result shape.

instructions_version.description: Notion setup instructions version, such as 0.0.2. Omit if unknown.

intent.description: One sentence: the wider task and why you chose this tool. Describe it in general terms. No names, page content, argument values, or secrets. English.

feedback.description: Only if an earlier Notion tool call in this task went wrong or fell short, pick the best fit: bug (a tool did the wrong thing), misleading_description (our tool text led you astray), missing_capability (our tools could not do the job), too_many_steps (you needed a workaround), opportunity (work stayed outside Notion that these tools could have handled). Otherwise omit.

skill.description: For tracking only: the name of the agent skill you are following for this task, such as notion-meeting-prep. Omit if you are not following a skill. Does not change what the tool does.

tools.name: DeferredToolPlaceholder
tools.description: Reserved placeholder that keeps deferred tool loading active; never call this tool.

tools.name: mcp__plugin_design_notion__notion-fetch
tools.description:
Retrieves details about a Notion entity (page, database, data source, or saved database view) by URL or ID.

id.description: The ID or URL of the Notion page, database, or data source to fetch. Supports notion.so URLs, Notion Sites URLs (*.notion.site), raw UUIDs, and data source URLs (collection://...). include_discussions.description: Whether to include discussion/comment indicators in the page output. When true, adds a <page-discussions> summary with discussion count, preview snippets, and discussion:// URLs. Use with the get_comments tool to retrieve full discussion content. Defaults to false.

include_file_urls.description: Whether to return signed download URLs for uploaded files. Defaults to false. When false, page Markdown cites uploaded files by stable notion-file-block:// references and the response has no references map; call get_file_download_urls with the references when you need those files' contents. When true, the response's references map gives the signed URL for each reference.

instructions_version.description: Notion setup instructions version, such as 0.0.2. Omit if unknown.

intent.description: One sentence: the wider task and why you chose this tool. Describe it in general terms. No names, page content, argument values, or secrets. English.

feedback.description: Only if an earlier Notion tool call in this task went wrong or fell short, pick the best fit: bug (a tool did the wrong thing), misleading_description (our tool text led you astray), missing_capability (our tools could not do the job), too_many_steps (you needed a workaround), opportunity (work stayed outside Notion that these tools could have handled). Otherwise omit.

skill.description: For tracking only: the name of the agent skill you are following for this task, such as notion-meeting-prep. Omit if you are not following a skill. Does not change what the tool does.

content.text: Tool loaded.

lastPrompt: keep the docs in the notion only

include_file_urls.description: Whether to return signed download URLs for uploaded files. Defaults to false. When false, page Markdown cites uploaded files by stable notion-file-block:// references and the response has no references map; call get_file_download_urls with the references when you need those files' contents. When true, the response's references map gives the signed URL for each reference.

instructions_version.description: Notion setup instructions version, such as 0.0.2. Omit if unknown.

intent.description: One sentence: the wider task and why you chose this tool. Describe it in general terms. No names, page content, argument values, or secrets. English.

feedback.description: Only if an earlier Notion tool call in this task went wrong or fell short, pick the best fit: bug (a tool did the wrong thing), misleading_description (our tool text led you astray), missing_capability (our tools could not do the job), too_many_steps (you needed a workaround), opportunity (work stayed outside Notion that these tools could have handled). Otherwise omit.

skill.description: For tracking only: the name of the agent skill you are following for this task, such as notion-meeting-prep. Omit if you are not following a skill. Does not change what the tool does.

The plan is sound in shape but wrong in one key place: the LoRA today learns Claude, not you. Build order is privacy and data hygiene first, then memory, then measured LoRA, then model choice — and nothing ships without a benchmark gate. ## 1. Is the thinking right? Mostly yes. Seven of ten ideas hold as stated; three need correcting before anything is built. | Your idea | Verdict | Why | | --- | --- | --- | | Recognise the user's patterns, keep only what matters, feed training and memory, then the model | Right | This is the correct order. The catch: the patterns must come from what *you* do (corrections, reverts, commits), not from what Claude wrote. | | More history gives a better LoRA | Wrong as stated | Quality beats volume. Rejected answers in the data teach the wrong habits. Also, Claude Code deletes old transcripts (about 30 days by default), so history shrinks unless we keep a copy. | | LoRA learns behaviour, memory holds facts | Right | Keep this split strictly. Anything you can write as a sentence belongs in memory, not in weights. | | Users state their preferences in prompts | Wrong for you | Measured on your history: zero recurring "always/never" statements. Your preferences show up as corrections ("why are we using local DB, use neon") and in repo config. | | Everything runs locally, including training | Right, with limits | On an 8 GB M1, only models up to about 3B (4-bit) can train. Training also heats the laptop, so it must run rarely and in the background. | | Evaluate higher precision and big models first (27B, 26B, Nemotron) | Not on this machine | None of these fit in 8 GB at any useful precision. This pillar needs a hardware decision first. | | BM25 plus semantic search | Right, later | BM25 already exists. Add embeddings only when an eval set shows BM25 missing relevant memories. | | One adapter per user per model | Right | Adapters don't transfer across model families. | | One memory schema for every model | Right | Memory is injected as plain text, so it already works with any model. | | Continuous automatic retraining | Later | Without an approval gate it can make the model worse silently. Build the gate first. | ## 2. Footprint today Today nearly all personalisation comes from text added to the prompt; the LoRA path exists but has barely been trained. Every line below was checked against the code on `main`. | Component | What it does | File | | --- | --- | --- | | Handover | At session start, adds the state of your last session in this project (goal, files, todos, last error, where it ended). Max 4000 chars, skipped if older than 7 days. Works for Claude Code and OpenCode. | `context.py`, `opencode_plugin.js` | | Recall memory | Every past task becomes `{prompt, files, cmds, outcome}`. On each prompt, BM25 (standard library) finds the top 3 similar tasks and adds them. Max 1500 chars, secrets redacted. | `memory.py` | | Session switch | Moves a Claude Code chat into OpenCode with full history. | `switch.py` | | Training data | `collect` turns every Claude assistant turn, plus up to 6000 chars before it, into one example. No filtering, no redaction. | `transcripts.py` | | LoRA training | `mlx_lm lora` on Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct-4bit, default rank and layers. Torch/PEFT on Linux and Windows (rank 8, alpha 16). | `backends/` | | Local server | OpenAI-compatible API on port 8399, auto-started by launchd/systemd. | `service.py` | | Bench | Replays your own finished tasks (ended in a commit and a passing check) with any model, memory on or off. Held-out sessions stay out of memory and training. | `bench.py` | | Vault | API keys plus `sync` of `data/` and `adapters/` to a private GitHub repo. | `vault.py` | | Website | Sign-in, API keys, setup steps, bench reports and share badges. | `UI-Web/` | **State of the data on this machine (measured 2026-11-03):** - `data/train.jsonl`: 3942 examples; 484 match a secret pattern. - Adapter: trained on Jul 15 for 100 iterations, about 2.5% of one pass over the data. It has learned almost nothing. - Bench: 1 qualifying task, so no reliable score yet. - Claude transcripts on disk: 30 sessions across 18 projects. ## 3. Gaps: today vs target The biggest gaps are in what the LoRA learns and in privacy; memory and evaluation are partly there. | Pillar | Exists today | Missing | Severity | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Privacy | Redaction in memory | Redaction in training data; `sync` uploads raw training data to GitHub | Critical | | Personalisation (LoRA) | Collect, train, serve | Trains on Claude's turns, including rejected ones. No accept/reject labels, no use of your own commits, custom tool format the client never uses, no versioning or rollback | High | | Personalisation (data) | Reads live transcripts | Own archive of transcripts, so history isn't lost after about 30 days | High | | Memory | Session memory (handover), task memory (BM25 recall) | User profile, project facts, corrections, scoring, merging, schema version | Medium | | Retrieval | BM25, same-project boost, fixed threshold | Embeddings, rank fusion, retrieval eval set | Low (until measured) | | Intelligence | One hard-coded model per platform | Model registry, switching, hardware check, per-model adapters | Medium | | Evaluation | Bench with memory on/off | Enough tasks (30+), personalisation metrics, LoRA arms, approval gate | High | | Isolation | One OS user = one `~/.footprint` | Fine for local use; nothing more needed now | None | ## 4. Target architecture Every session passes one labeller; its labels decide what becomes training data and what becomes memory. The model sits at the end and can be swapped. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Claude Code sessions] --> D B[OpenCode sessions] --> D C[Git history, repo config] --> D D["Archive and redact
local copy kept; secrets removed first"] --> E E["Pattern labeller
each task: accepted, rejected or user-authored"] --> F E --> G F["Curated training data
accepted work only, split by session"] --> H G["Structured memory
profile, project, session, task history"] --> I H["LoRA adapter
per user, per model; versioned"] -- "if it passes the bench gate" --> J I["Context builder
BM25 top matches, ~1500-token budget"] -- "selected context only" --> J J["Active model
local Qwen with its adapter, or any cloud model"] style E fill:#e7f1fb,stroke:#2b6cb0,stroke-width:2px ``` Memory reaches every model as text. The adapter reaches only the local model it was trained for, and only after it passes the bench gate. Cloud models get memory only. ## 5. The pipeline, stage by stage One pipeline reads each session once and produces two separate outputs: curated training data and structured memory. The pattern labeller in the middle is the core of the whole system. | # | Stage | Input | Output | Rule | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | Archive | Claude Code `.jsonl`, OpenCode DB | Local copy in `~/.footprint/archive/` | Copy every session as soon as it ends. Never depend on Claude Code keeping it. | | 2 | Redact | Archived session | Same session, secrets replaced | Runs before anything else reads the data. Nothing unredacted leaves this stage. | | 3 | Segment | Session | Tasks: one real prompt plus everything until the next | Already exists in `memory.py`. | | 4 | Label (pattern recognition) | Task + the user's next prompt + git history | `accepted`, `rejected`, `user-authored`, or `unknown` | See the signal table below. | | 5a | Curate for training | Accepted and user-authored tasks | `train / valid / test` split by session, newest = test | Cap examples per session; remove near-duplicates. | | 5b | Extract for memory | All labelled tasks + repo config | Memory records (section 6) | Merge repeats, track evidence and confidence. | | 6 | Use | Memory records, adapter | Context for the active model | Model-independent text; adapter only for its own model. | **Signals the labeller uses:** | Signal | Label | Measured on your history | | --- | --- | --- | | Your next prompt pushes back ("no…", "still broken", "why are we using X") | rejected | 59 of about 1160 turns | | You interrupted the answer | rejected | included above | | You moved on to a new ask | accepted (weak) | most turns | | AI edit survives into a commit | accepted (strong) | not built yet | | `git checkout` / `git restore` right after an AI edit | rejected (strong) | not built yet | | Code you committed that no AI edit produced | user-authored (best style signal) | not built yet | The last three need git, not chat. They are the most reliable signals, and the hardest part to build. ## 6. Memory design One record format for all four categories, stored as local JSON. Retrieval decides what reaches the prompt, under a fixed budget of about 1500 tokens. **The four categories and where each comes from:** | Category | Holds | Source | When injected | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | User profile | Languages, formatter, test command, commit style, package manager | Repo config files and git log, not chat | Session start | | Project memory | Stack, DB, deploy target, decisions ("Neon, not local DB") | Corrections + repo files | Session start, this project only | | Session memory | Current goal, files touched, open todos, last error | Last session (exists: handover) | Session start | | Task history | Past tasks, how they ended, what you corrected | Labelled tasks (exists: recall) | Each prompt, top 3 by relevance | **Record schema (v1):** ```json { "id": "m_8f2c1a9e", "schema": 1, "kind": "project_fact", "scope": "project:/Users/aman/Developer/Paytmcall", "text": "Use Neon Postgres, not a local DB", "source": "correction", "evidence": ["ses_ab12:t4", "ses_cd34:t1"], "count": 2, "confidence": 0.65, "first_seen": "2026-10-02", "last_seen": "2026-11-01", "supersedes": null } ``` - `kind`: `profile` | `project_fact` | `decision` | `correction` | `task`. - `source`: `config` | `git` | `correction` | `stated` — how we know it. Config and git rank highest. - Same fact seen again: add evidence, raise confidence. A newer fact that contradicts an older one sets `supersedes`; the old one stops being injected but is kept. - Inject only facts seen at least twice, or read from config. Seen once means a one-off task, not a habit. **Retrieval:** filter by project, then BM25 (exists). Add embeddings and rank fusion only after a retrieval eval set shows BM25 missing relevant records. No vector database: SQLite with full-text search is enough at this size. **Why the schema works across models:** records become plain text in the prompt. Any model, local or cloud, reads text. Nothing in memory depends on the model. ## 7. LoRA design The LoRA should learn how you work — code shape, naming, the order you read, edit and test — from evidence you accepted. It should not learn facts; memory carries those. **What goes into training:** | Example type | Input | Target | Status | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Accepted turn | Prompt + context | Assistant turn you didn't push back on | Prototype built | | Committed diff | Task prompt + file before | Diff that reached a commit | To build | | Your own code | Commit message + file before | Your hand-written change | To build, best style signal | | Rejected turn | — | Excluded now; saved as pairs for preference training later | Prototype excludes it | **Training setup (starting point, change only on measured gain):** - Base model: the active model from the registry (section 8), not hard-coded. - Format: the model's native chat template and native tool-call format. Today's custom `` format is never used by OpenCode at runtime, so the adapter learns a protocol nobody speaks. - Loss on the assistant's tokens only (`--mask-prompt` in mlx-lm). - Rank 8–16, alpha 2× rank, attention and MLP layers, 1–2 passes, stop early on validation loss. - Run in the background at low priority, only on new data, at most weekly. Training heats the laptop. **Versioning and approval:** ``` adapters//v3/adapters.safetensors adapters//v3/metrics.json # data hash, loss, bench scores adapters//active -> v2 # switch only after the gate passes ``` Rollback means pointing `active` back to an earlier version. A new version becomes active only if it passes the gate in section 9. **Honest expectation:** on a 1.5B–3B model, a LoRA will not match a cloud model at finishing tasks. Its realistic value is style and convention. If the bench shows no gain over memory alone, keep LoRA optional. ## 8. Intelligence layer Pick the model last, behind a small registry, so memory and the pipeline never depend on it. The hardware decides which models are even possible. **Model registry (one small file, no framework):** ```json {"active": "qwen2.5-coder-1.5b", "models": { "qwen2.5-coder-1.5b": {"mlx": "mlx-community/Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct-4bit", "min_ram_gb": 8, "trainable": true} }} ``` `footprint model use ` switches the active model, and its adapter if one exists for that model. Memory is unchanged. Cloud models (Big Pickle, GLM, Gemini) get memory but no adapter. **What fits in memory (approximate: weights only, about 2 bytes per parameter at bf16 and about 0.55 at 4-bit):** | Model size | bf16 weights | 4-bit weights | 8 GB M1: run | 8 GB M1: train LoRA | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1.5B | ~3 GB | ~0.9 GB | Yes | Yes | | 3–4B | ~7 GB | ~2 GB | 4-bit only | 4-bit, tight | | 9B | ~18 GB | ~5 GB | 4-bit, very tight | No | | 26–31B | ~55–62 GB | ~15–17 GB | No | No | Only about 5–6 GB of the 8 GB is usable after macOS. So on this machine, quantisation is not optional above about 2B. "Higher precision first" needs 32 GB or more. **Candidates from the proposal (names, sizes and licences still to verify before use):** - Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B — current baseline, fits today. - Qwen3.5 9B and 27B — 9B is the realistic upgrade on a 16–32 GB machine. - Gemma 4 — check whether a 12B exists; the 26B A4B mixture-of-experts still needs all weights in memory. - NVIDIA Nemotron — check which coding checkpoint and its licence. Decide with the bench, not with leaderboards: same tasks, same memory, each model. ## 9. Evaluation Nothing is called an improvement until the bench shows it. The bench already exists; it needs more tasks and personalisation metrics. **Experiments (same tasks, same repo state, same tools):** | Run | Memory | LoRA | Answers | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | A | off | off | Baseline | | B | on | off | What memory adds | | C | off | on | What LoRA adds | | D | on | on | Combined | **Metrics:** | Group | Metric | How measured | | --- | --- | --- | | Coding | Task pass rate | Bench: the original check passes and at least one file changed | | Personalisation | Style match | Lint and format errors of the model's diff against the repo's own config | | Personalisation | Closeness to your accepted change | Edit distance to the diff you actually committed | | Personalisation | Correction rate in real use | Corrective follow-up prompts per task, read from logs (labeller from section 5) | | Memory | Retrieval hit rate | Was the relevant past task in the top 3? Needs a small labelled set | | System | Latency, peak RAM, training time | Logged per run | **Approval gate for a new adapter:** - [ ] Validation loss lower than the active adapter on the session-split test set - [ ] Bench pass rate not lower than the active adapter - [ ] Style match not worse - [ ] At least 30 bench tasks, so the numbers mean something **Data rules:** the newest sessions are the test set and are never trained on. Bench tasks are held out from memory and training (already true). ## 10. Roadmap Five phases in strict order; each starts only when the previous gate passes. Phase 1 is small and removes the privacy risk, so it comes first. ```mermaid flowchart TD P1["1. Data hygiene (start here)
Redact training data; split by session
Keep data local; archive transcripts"] --> G1{{"Gate: 0 secret hits; archive captures every new session"}} G1 --> P2["2. Labeller and bench
Accept/reject labels from chat and git
Grow the bench to 30+ tasks; style and correction metrics"] P2 --> G2{{"Gate: labels spot-checked on 50 tasks; bench has 30+ tasks"}} G2 --> P3["3. Memory facts
Profile from repo config and git; facts from corrections
Merge, supersede, inject under a budget"] P3 --> G3{{"Gate: experiment B (memory) beats A"}} G3 --> P4["4. LoRA v2
Native chat and tool format; accepted turns + your commits
Versioned adapters, rollback, background training"] P4 --> G4{{"Gate: C or D beats B; adapter passes approval checks"}} G4 --> P5["5. Model choice
Registry and switching; hardware decision first
Compare on the same bench and memory"] P5 --> G5{{"Gate: the bench picks the default model"}} style P1 fill:#e7f1fb,stroke:#2b6cb0,stroke-width:2px ``` Phase 2 is the hardest: git-based labels (commits, reverts, your own code) are the most reliable signal and the most work. If phase 3 gives most of the gain, phase 4 can wait. ## 11. Open decisions These decide scope; building before answering them risks rework. - [ ] **Target hardware.** Stay on 8 GB M1 (models up to about 3B, 4-bit), or plan for 32 GB or more? Decides the whole model pillar. - [ ] **Who is the user?** Only you, or other developers through tracefootprint.space? Decides how much setup and isolation work is needed. - [ ] **Training data in the vault.** Never synced, synced encrypted, or synced as today? - [ ] **What the LoRA imitates.** Your accepted and committed work only (recommended), or Claude's style too? - [ ] **Is LoRA required at all?** If memory alone gives most of the gain on the bench, should LoRA stay an optional extra? - [ ] **Model licences.** Which licences are acceptable if footprint is offered to others? ## 12. Prototype already built A first cut of stages 2, 4 and 5 exists on branch `worktree-distill-pipeline`, pushed but **not merged**. Treat it as a spike that tested the ideas, not as the build. | Part | Result on your data | | --- | --- | | Redaction in `collect` | Secret-pattern hits went from 484 to 0 | | Correction labeller | 59 rejected turns found and dropped; 1104 accepted examples kept | | Session-based split | Train, valid and test no longer share sessions | | Preference extraction from prompts | Found no recurring preferences: you correct rather than state. This changed the memory design in section 6 | | `sync` | Training data stays local unless `--with-data` | Recommendation: after the decisions above, merge the redaction, split and `sync` parts as they are (low risk), and redo the rest following this plan.

Build order is privacy and data hygiene first, then memory, then measured LoRA, then model choice — and nothing ships without a benchmark gate. ## 1. Is the thinking right? Mostly yes. Seven of ten ideas hold as stated; three need correcting before anything is built. | Your idea | Verdict | Why | | --- | --- | --- | | Recognise the user's patterns, keep only what matters, feed training and memory, then the model | Right | This is the correct order. The catch: the patterns must come from what you do (corrections, reverts, commits), not from what Claude wrote. | | More history gives a better LoRA | Wrong as stated | Quality beats volume. Rejected answers in the data teach the wrong habits. Also, Claude Code deletes old transcripts (about 30 days by default), so history shrinks unless we keep a copy. | | LoRA learns behaviour, memory holds facts | Right | Keep this split strictly. Anything you can write as a sentence belongs in memory, not in weights. | | Users state their preferences in prompts | Wrong for you | Measured on your history: zero recurring "always/never" statements. Your preferences show up as corrections ("why are we using local DB, use neon") and in repo config. | | Everything runs locally, including training | Right, with limits | On an 8 GB M1, only models up to about 3B (4-bit) can train. Training also heats the laptop, so it must run rarely and in the background. | | Evaluate higher precision and big models first (27B, 26B, Nemotron) | Not on this machine | None of these fit in 8 GB at any useful precision. This pillar needs a hardware decision first. | | BM25 plus semantic search | Right, later | BM25 already exists. Add embeddings only when an eval set shows BM25 missing relevant memories. | | One adapter per user per model | Right | Adapters don't transfer across model families. | | One memory schema for every model | Right | Memory is injected as plain text, so it already works with any model. | | Continuous automatic retraining | Later | Without an approval gate it can make the model worse silently. Build the gate first. | ## 2. Footprint today Today nearly all personalisation comes from text added to the prompt; the LoRA path exists but has barely been trained. Every line below was checked against the code on main. | Component | What it does | File | | --- | --- | --- | | Handover | At session start, adds the state of your last session in this project (goal, files, todos, last error, where it ended). Max 4000 chars, skipped if older than 7 days. Works for Claude Code and OpenCode. | context.py, opencode_plugin.js | | Recall memory | Every past task becomes {prompt, files, cmds, outcome}. On each prompt, BM25 (standard library) finds the top 3 similar tasks and adds them. Max 1500 chars, secrets redacted. | memory.py | | Session switch | Moves a Claude Code chat into OpenCode with full history. | switch.py | | Training data | collect turns every Claude assistant turn, plus up to 6000 chars before it, into one example. No filtering, no redaction. | transcripts.py | | LoRA training | mlx_lm lora on Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct-4bit, default rank and layers. Torch/PEFT on Linux and Windows (rank 8, alpha 16). | backends/ | | Local server | OpenAI-compatible API on port 8399, auto-started by launchd/systemd. | service.py | | Bench | Replays your own finished tasks (ended in a commit and a passing check) with any model, memory on or off. Held-out sessions stay out of memory and training. | bench.py | | Vault | API keys plus sync of data/ and adapters/ to a private GitHub repo. | vault.py | | Website | Sign-in, API keys, setup steps, bench reports and share badges. | UI-Web/ | State of the data on this machine (measured 2026-11-03): - data/train.jsonl: 3942 examples; 484 match a secret pattern. - Adapter: trained on Jul 15 for 100 iterations, about 2.5% of one pass over the data. It has learned almost nothing. - Bench: 1 qualifying task, so no reliable score yet. - Claude transcripts on disk: 30 sessions across 18 projects. ## 3. Gaps: today vs target The biggest gaps are in what the LoRA learns and in privacy; memory and evaluation are partly there. | Pillar | Exists today | Missing | Severity | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Privacy | Redaction in memory | Redaction in training data; sync uploads raw training data to GitHub | Critical | | Personalisation (LoRA) | Collect, train, serve | Trains on Claude's turns, including rejected ones. No accept/reject labels, no use of your own commits, custom tool format the client never uses, no versioning or rollback | High | | Personalisation (data) | Reads live transcripts | Own archive of transcripts, so history isn't lost after about 30 days | High | | Memory | Session memory (handover), task memory (BM25 recall) | User profile, project facts, corrections, scoring, merging, schema version | Medium | | Retrieval | BM25, same-project boost, fixed threshold | Embeddings, rank fusion, retrieval eval set | Low (until measured) | | Intelligence | One hard-coded model per platform | Model registry, switching, hardware check, per-model adapters | Medium | | Evaluation | Bench with memory on/off | Enough tasks (30+), personalisation metrics, LoRA arms, approval gate | High | | Isolation | One OS user = one ~/.footprint | Fine for local use; nothing more needed now | None | ## 4. Target architecture Every session passes one labeller; its labels decide what becomes training data and what becomes memory. The model sits at the end and can be swapped. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[Claude Code sessions] --> D B[OpenCode sessions] --> D C[Git history, repo config] --> D D["Archive and redact
local copy kept; secrets removed first"] --> E E["Pattern labeller
each task: accepted, rejected or user-authored"] --> F E --> G F["Curated training data
accepted work only, split by session"] --> H G["Structured memory
profile, project, session, task history"] --> I H["LoRA adapter
per user, per model; versioned"] -- "if it passes the bench gate" --> J I["Context builder
BM25 top matches, ~1500-token budget"] -- "selected context only" --> J J["Active model
local Qwen with its adapter, or any cloud model"] style E fill:#e7f1fb,stroke:#2b6cb0,stroke-width:2px ``` Memory reaches every model as text. The adapter reaches only the local model it was trained for, and only after it passes the bench gate. Cloud models get memory only. ## 5. The pipeline, stage by stage One pipeline reads each session once and produces two separate outputs: curated training data and structured memory. The pattern labeller in the middle is the core of the whole system. | # | Stage | Input | Output | Rule | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1 | Archive | Claude Code .jsonl, OpenCode DB | Local copy in ~/.footprint/archive/ | Copy every session as soon as it ends. Never depend on Claude Code keeping it. | | 2 | Redact | Archived session | Same session, secrets replaced | Runs before anything else reads the data. Nothing unredacted leaves this stage. | | 3 | Segment | Session | Tasks: one real prompt plus everything until the next | Already exists in memory.py. | | 4 | Label (pattern recognition) | Task + the user's next prompt + git history | accepted, rejected, user-authored, or unknown | See the signal table below. | | 5a | Curate for training | Accepted and user-authored tasks | train / valid / test split by session, newest = test | Cap examples per session; remove near-duplicates. | | 5b | Extract for memory | All labelled tasks + repo config | Memory records (section 6) | Merge repeats, track evidence and confidence. | | 6 | Use | Memory records, adapter | Context for the active model | Model-independent text; adapter only for its own model. | Signals the labeller uses: | Signal | Label | Measured on your history | | --- | --- | --- | | Your next prompt pushes back ("no…", "still broken", "why are we using X") | rejected | 59 of about 1160 turns | | You interrupted the answer | rejected | included above | | You moved on to a new ask | accepted (weak) | most turns | | AI edit survives into a commit | accepted (strong) | not built yet | | git checkout / git restore right after an AI edit | rejected (strong) | not built yet | | Code you committed that no AI edit produced | user-authored (best style signal) | not built yet | The last three need git, not chat. They are the most reliable signals, and the hardest part to build. ## 6. Memory design One record format for all four categories, stored as local JSON. Retrieval decides what reaches the prompt, under a fixed budget of about 1500 tokens. The four categories and where each comes from: | Category | Holds | Source | When injected | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | User profile | Languages, formatter, test command, commit style, package manager | Repo config files and git log, not chat | Session start | | Project memory | Stack, DB, deploy target, decisions ("Neon, not local DB") | Corrections + repo files | Session start, this project only | | Session memory | Current goal, files touched, open todos, last error | Last session (exists: handover) | Session start | | Task history | Past tasks, how they ended, what you corrected | Labelled tasks (exists: recall) | Each prompt, top 3 by relevance | Record schema (v1): ```json { "id": "m_8f2c1a9e", "schema": 1, "kind": "project_fact", "scope": "project:/Users/aman/Developer/Paytmcall", "text": "Use Neon Postgres, not a local DB", "source": "correction", "evidence": ["ses_ab12:t4", "ses_cd34:t1"], "count": 2, "confidence": 0.65, "first_seen": "2026-10-02", "last_seen": "2026-11-01", "supersedes": null } ``` - kind: profile \| project_fact \| decision \| correction \| task. - source: config \| git \| correction \| stated — how we know it. Config and git rank highest. - Same fact seen again: add evidence, raise confidence. A newer fact that contradicts an older one sets supersedes; the old one stops being injected but is kept. - Inject only facts seen at least twice, or read from config. Seen once means a one-off task, not a habit. Retrieval: filter by project, then BM25 (exists). Add embeddings and rank fusion only after a retrieval eval set shows BM25 missing relevant records. No vector database: SQLite with full-text search is enough at this size. Why the schema works across models: records become plain text in the prompt. Any model, local or cloud, reads text. Nothing in memory depends on the model. ## 7. LoRA design The LoRA should learn how you work — code shape, naming, the order you read, edit and test — from evidence you accepted. It should not learn facts; memory carries those. What goes into training: | Example type | Input | Target | Status | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Accepted turn | Prompt + context | Assistant turn you didn't push back on | Prototype built | | Committed diff | Task prompt + file before | Diff that reached a commit | To build | | Your own code | Commit message + file before | Your hand-written change | To build, best style signal | | Rejected turn | — | Excluded now; saved as pairs for preference training later | Prototype excludes it | Training setup (starting point, change only on measured gain): - Base model: the active model from the registry (section 8), not hard-coded. - Format: the model's native chat template and native tool-call format. Today's custom format is never used by OpenCode at runtime, so the adapter learns a protocol nobody speaks. - Loss on the assistant's tokens only (--mask-prompt in mlx-lm). - Rank 8–16, alpha 2× rank, attention and MLP layers, 1–2 passes, stop early on validation loss. - Run in the background at low priority, only on new data, at most weekly. Training heats the laptop. Versioning and approval: ```javascript adapters//v3/adapters.safetensors adapters//v3/metrics.json # data hash, loss, bench scores adapters//active -> v2 # switch only after the gate passes ``` Rollback means pointing active back to an earlier version. A new version becomes active only if it passes the gate in section 9. Honest expectation: on a 1.5B–3B model, a LoRA will not match a cloud model at finishing tasks. Its realistic value is style and convention. If the bench shows no gain over memory alone, keep LoRA optional. ## 8. Intelligence layer Pick the model last, behind a small registry, so memory and the pipeline never depend on it. The hardware decides which models are even possible. Model registry (one small file, no framework): ```json {"active": "qwen2.5-coder-1.5b", "models": { "qwen2.5-coder-1.5b": {"mlx": "mlx-community/Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B-Instruct-4bit", "min_ram_gb": 8, "trainable": true} }} ``` footprint model use switches the active model, and its adapter if one exists for that model. Memory is unchanged. Cloud models (Big Pickle, GLM, Gemini) get memory but no adapter. What fits in memory (approximate: weights only, about 2 bytes per parameter at bf16 and about 0.55 at 4-bit): | Model size | bf16 weights | 4-bit weights | 8 GB M1: run | 8 GB M1: train LoRA | | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | | 1.5B | \~3 GB | \~0.9 GB | Yes | Yes | | 3–4B | \~7 GB | \~2 GB | 4-bit only | 4-bit, tight | | 9B | \~18 GB | \~5 GB | 4-bit, very tight | No | | 26–31B | \~55–62 GB | \~15–17 GB | No | No | Only about 5–6 GB of the 8 GB is usable after macOS. So on this machine, quantisation is not optional above about 2B. "Higher precision first" needs 32 GB or more. Candidates from the proposal (names, sizes and licences still to verify before use): - Qwen2.5-Coder-1.5B — current baseline, fits today. - Qwen3.5 9B and 27B — 9B is the realistic upgrade on a 16–32 GB machine. - Gemma 4 — check whether a 12B exists; the 26B A4B mixture-of-experts still needs all weights in memory. - NVIDIA Nemotron — check which coding checkpoint and its licence. Decide with the bench, not with leaderboards: same tasks, same memory, each model. ## 9. Evaluation Nothing is called an improvement until the bench shows it. The bench already exists; it needs more tasks and personalisation metrics. Experiments (same tasks, same repo state, same tools): | Run | Memory | LoRA | Answers | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | A | off | off | Baseline | | B | on | off | What memory adds | | C | off | on | What LoRA adds | | D | on | on | Combined | Metrics: | Group | Metric | How measured | | --- | --- | --- | | Coding | Task pass rate | Bench: the original check passes and at least one file changed | | Personalisation | Style match | Lint and format errors of the model's diff against the repo's own config | | Personalisation | Closeness to your accepted change | Edit distance to the diff you actually committed | | Personalisation | Correction rate in real use | Corrective follow-up prompts per task, read from logs (labeller from section 5) | | Memory | Retrieval hit rate | Was the relevant past task in the top 3? Needs a small labelled set | | System | Latency, peak RAM, training time | Logged per run | Approval gate for a new adapter: - [ ] Validation loss lower than the active adapter on the session-split test set - [ ] Bench pass rate not lower than the active adapter - [ ] Style match not worse - [ ] At least 30 bench tasks, so the numbers mean something Data rules: the newest sessions are the test set and are never trained on. Bench tasks are held out from memory and training (already true). ## 10. Roadmap Five phases in strict order; each starts only when the previous gate passes. Phase 1 is small and removes the privacy risk, so it comes first. ```mermaid flowchart TD P1["1. Data hygiene (start here)
Redact training data; split by session
Keep data local; archive transcripts"] --> G1{{"Gate: 0 secret hits; archive captures every new session"}} G1 --> P2["2. Labeller and bench
Accept/reject labels from chat and git
Grow the bench to 30+ tasks; style and correction metrics"] P2 --> G2{{"Gate: labels spot-checked on 50 tasks; bench has 30+ tasks"}} G2 --> P3["3. Memory facts
Profile from repo config and git; facts from corrections
Merge, supersede, inject under a budget"] P3 --> G3{{"Gate: experiment B (memory) beats A"}} G3 --> P4["4. LoRA v2
Native chat and tool format; accepted turns + your commits
Versioned adapters, rollback, background training"] P4 --> G4{{"Gate: C or D beats B; adapter passes approval checks"}} G4 --> P5["5. Model choice
Registry and switching; hardware decision first
Compare on the same bench and memory"] P5 --> G5{{"Gate: the bench picks the default model"}} style P1 fill:#e7f1fb,stroke:#2b6cb0,stroke-width:2px ``` Phase 2 is the hardest: git-based labels (commits, reverts, your own code) are the most reliable signal and the most work. If phase 3 gives most of the gain, phase 4 can wait. ## 11. Open decisions These decide scope; building before answering them risks rework. - [ ] Target hardware. Stay on 8 GB M1 (models up to about 3B, 4-bit), or plan for 32 GB or more? Decides the whole model pillar. - [ ] Who is the user? Only you, or other developers through [tracefootprint.space](http://tracefootprint.space)? Decides how much setup and isolation work is needed. - [ ] Training data in the vault. Never synced, synced encrypted, or synced as today? - [ ] What the LoRA imitates. Your accepted and committed work only (recommended), or Claude's style too? - [ ] Is LoRA required at all? If memory alone gives most of the gain on the bench, should LoRA stay an optional extra? - [ ] Model licences. Which licences are acceptable if footprint is offered to others? ## 12. Prototype already built A first cut of stages 2, 4 and 5 exists on branch worktree-distill-pipeline, pushed but not merged. Treat it as a spike that tested the ideas, not as the build. | Part | Result on your data | | --- | --- | | Redaction in collect | Secret-pattern hits went from 484 to 0 | | Correction labeller | 59 rejected turns found and dropped; 1104 accepted examples kept | | Session-based split | Train, valid and test no longer share sessions | | Preference extraction from prompts | Found no recurring preferences: you correct rather than state. This changed the memory design in section 6 | | sync | Training data stays local unless --with-data | Recommendation: after the decisions above, merge the redaction, split and sync parts as they are (low risk), and redo the rest following this plan. Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

A task with "multiple angles," "thorough," or several parts is not a request to spawn; handle it inline with your own tools. Only use this tool when the user explicitly says to use a subagent, or names one of the available agent types.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- The agent's final report is not shown to the user — relay what matters.
- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- When you fan work out in parallel, give each independent lookup `effort: "lower"` — that is where the step cheaper pays most. More generally, pass `"lower"` for any mechanical, self-checking brief (find-and-report, grep across named files, a pattern you spelled out); pass `"higher"` for a well-specified piece that needs more reasoning than the work around it.
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.
