entries.description:
Update a Notion page's properties, content, icon, or cover. For only an icon or cover, use "update_properties" without "properties".

## Core rules

**IMPORTANT**: Before writing page content, read the MCP resource `notion://docs/notion-flavored-markdown-spec` through your MCP client's resource-reading interface, or call the Notion "fetch" tool with this URI if your client does not support reading MCP resources. Do NOT pass this URI to any other URL-fetching tool. Don't guess Markdown syntax. By default, use native Notion mentions for references you add to existing Notion pages, databases, data sources, people, and dates. Use Markdown links only for external URLs or when the user requests a plain link. For a person, use a user mention with their user URL, found with search using query_type "user"; do not write "@Name" as plain text. For a specific date or time, such as a due date or meeting time, use a date mention. The Markdown specification gives the mention syntax.

Before changing content, fetch unless already loaded. Match nearby headings, block types, nesting, lists, tables, and prose style.

Make the smallest edit. Use "update_content" for targeted search-and-replace and "insert_content" only to prepend or append. Avoid "replace_content" when a targeted command works. Preserve unrelated wording, structure, order, and native references. Do not broadly rewrite unless asked.

For "update_content", use the smallest exact old_str that uniquely matches the target. Ask before removing material content the user did not identify. Don't fetch just to verify an update that completed without warnings. Fetch to resolve warnings, or when a later step needs the page's exact saved state.

For "replace_content", preserve child pages and databases with their exact fetched tags. If validation says child content would be deleted, show the list and ask first. Never retry with "allow_deleting_content": true without confirmation. Report any "warnings" in the result.

page_id.description: The page ID, with or without dashes, or a Notion page URL.

properties.description:
Used by the "update_properties" command, and required unless "icon", "cover", or "is_skill" is set. A JSON object that updates the page's properties.
For pages in a database, fetch the page or its data source first and use the exact property names and SQLite schema definition shown in <database>.
For page titles outside a database, use "title" in inline Markdown.
For a Files property, an uploaded file can be provided as {"type":"file_upload","file_upload":{"id":"<file-upload-id>"}} inside the property's array.

So about 97% of the talk never becomes a rule. That's the "less data" you want.

## How a sentence becomes a rule

Memory has three tiers:

1. **Raw archive.** Everything, redacted. Never injected; only used to rebuild the rest.
2. **Task history.** One small record per task: what you asked, the files touched, how it ended, what you corrected. Retrieved only when a new prompt is similar (top 3).
3. **Rules.** Promoted only with evidence. Injected at the start of every session, under a fixed budget.

What earns promotion to a rule, strongest first:

| Evidence | Why it counts |
|---|---|
| Repo config or git (`pnpm-lock.yaml`, `.prettierrc`, test script, commit style) | It's what you actually do. No talk needed. |
| A correction | You rejected something and named what you want. |
| The same instruction in 2+ sessions | Repetition means a habit, not a one-off. |
| An approach that ended in a commit plus a passing check | It's a proven solution. |

What demotes a rule: a newer correction that contradicts it (it gets marked "superseded" and stops being injected), or no use for a long time.

## How we tell vague from important
Rules first, cheap and local:
- **Correction:** pushback words at the start, or an interrupt.
- **Ack:** short and from an ack list.
- **Paste:** fenced or JSON text, or very long.
- **Question:** ends in "?" or starts with how/what/why/can.
- **Everything else** is an instruction.

The small local model is used only for unclear cases, and only if the rules prove too noisy.

## Honest limit: "100% of the user's pattern" can't be measured as a number
What we *can* measure:
- **Rule precision:** of the promoted rules, how many are actually right. Target ≥90%, checked by hand on 50 rules.
- **Correction rate:** with memory on, do you have to say "no, use X" less often? This is the real test that the pattern was learned.

content.text:
"Ack" is short for **acknowledgement**: a short reply that only says "yes, go on" and carries no new information.

Examples from your messages: "ok do it", "cool", "yes", "go ahead", "push it", "thanks".

**Why memory treats it specially:**
- **As content, it's worthless.** "ok do it" says nothing about how you code, so it never becomes a rule.
- **As a signal, it's useful.** It means you **accepted** Claude's previous answer, so that answer gets labelled "accepted" and can be used as good training data.

So an ack is never stored itself; it just marks the answer before it as approved.

The plan uses the jargon "Ack". I can rename it there to **"Approval (ok / yes / do it)"** so it reads clearly.

content.text:
## What LoRA is, simply
The base model (Qwen) stays frozen. LoRA trains a small add-on, about 0.1–1% extra weights, that nudges its answers toward your examples. The result is one small file: yours is 21 MB, loaded on top of the model when it runs.

## How our LoRA design would work
1. **Pick examples:** only work you accepted. That means turns you didn't push back on, diffs that reached a commit, and code you wrote yourself. Rejected turns are dropped.
2. **Format:** write each example in the model's own chat and tool-call format, so training matches how OpenCode actually calls it.
3. **Train:** `mlx_lm lora`, with loss counted only on the assistant's part. Small rank, 1–2 passes, in the background.
4. **Version:** `adapters/<model>/v3/`, next to its scores.
5. **Gate:** it becomes active only if the bench shows it beats memory alone. Otherwise it stays off.

## Why we would need it
For **habits that are hard to put in words**: code shape, naming, how big a change is, the order of read → edit → test. Memory is better for anything you can say as a sentence.

## The catch
- It only works on the **local model it was trained for**. Big Pickle, GLM and Gemini can't use it.
- It's **small-model only** on your 8 GB machine (about 3B max), and those models are weaker than cloud models at finishing tasks.
- It **needs retraining** for every new model, every time.
- With about 1100 good examples, expect a gain in style, not in getting tasks done.

## Alternatives, compared

| Option | How it works | Works with any model? | Training? | Expected result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Your own past code as examples** | Put 1–2 of your accepted diffs for similar tasks into the prompt | Yes | No | **High.** Models copy style well from examples. |
| **Generated rules file** (`AGENTS.md`) | Turn memory rules into a file OpenCode reads automatically | Yes | No | High for stated rules, nearly free. |
| **Formatter/linter after each edit** | Run your prettier/eslint/ruff config on the model's output | Yes | No | **100% for formatting and lint style**, guaranteed. |
| Memory (planned) | Rules plus similar past tasks in context | Yes | No | High for facts and decisions. |
| LoRA | Weights nudged toward your examples | Local model only | Yes, per model | Medium; style only. |
| Preference training (DPO) | Learns accepted vs rejected pairs | Local model only | Yes, needs more data | Later, maybe. |
| Bigger base model | More raw ability | — | No | Big gain in task success, but needs more RAM. |

## Recommendation
For your goal (any model carries on your work when Claude runs out), the top three alternatives beat LoRA:
1. **Formatter hook:** guarantees style, cheapest.
2. **Your own diffs as examples:** captures the shape of your code without training.
3. **`AGENTS.md` generated from memory:** rules every model reads.

Keep LoRA as an **optional experiment** behind the bench gate. Build it only if memory plus examples still leaves a measurable gap.

Section 7 of the Notion plan doesn't have this comparison yet. Should I add it?

content.text:
Here's memory end to end. I'll follow one real message of yours through the whole pipeline.

## The worked example
In Paytmcall you typed: **"why are we using local DB , use neon"**

### Step 1: Ingest and redact
- The session file is copied into the archive, and secrets are stripped first.
- Nothing downstream ever sees an unredacted line.

### Step 2: Segment into tasks
- The session is split at each real prompt.
- Your previous ask ("first we need to run this in local and test…") plus Claude's work on it make up **task A**.
- Your "why are we using local DB" message starts **task B**.

### Step 3: Classify each message
Cheap rules, no model:
- Starts with "why are we using…" → **Correction**.
- So task A is labelled **rejected** and gets `corrected: "why are we using local DB, use neon"`.

### Step 4: Extract a candidate rule
- **Text:** your own words, kept as they are: "use neon, not local DB". No rewording, so nothing can be made up. A local model may tidy the wording later, but only if needed.
- **Scope:** `project:/Users/aman/Developer/Paytmcall`, because it was said in that project.
- **Source:** `correction`.

### Step 5: Merge with what already exists
- The meaningful words (`neon`, `local`, `db`) are compared with existing rules in the same scope.
- **Same rule found** (enough shared words): add this session to `evidence`; `seen_in_sessions` goes 1 → 2.
- **Same subject, opposite choice** (e.g. an older "use local sqlite"): the newer one wins, and the old one gets `superseded`.
- **No match:** stored as a new candidate with `seen_in_sessions: 1`.

### Step 6: Score it
```
score = source weight × repetition × recency
source:     config 1.0 · git 0.9 · correction 0.8 · stated 0.5
repetition: min(1, seen_in_sessions / 3)
recency:    halves every ~60 days without being seen again
```
- A correction seen in 2 sessions scores 0.8 × 0.67 ≈ 0.53, which is above the injection line.
- Seen once, it scores 0.27 and is stored but **not injected**.

### Step 7: Store
```
~/.footprint/archive/        raw sessions, redacted (never injected)
~/.footprint/memory.json     task history index (exists today)
~/.footprint/rules.json      promoted rules, schema v1 (to build)
<repo>/AGENTS.md             a generated block of this project's rules, between markers
```
- The `AGENTS.md` block sits between markers, so your own text in that file is never touched.
- Any model that reads `AGENTS.md` gets the rules, even without footprint's hooks.

### Step 8: Use it, on a budget
- **Session start**, about 1200 tokens total:
  - Rules: up to about 400 tokens, highest score first, this project plus user-wide.
  - Handover: up to about 800 tokens.
- **Every prompt**, about 800 tokens:
  - The top 3 similar past tasks (BM25, already built), each with "user then corrected: …".
  - 1–2 of your own accepted diffs for similar work, about 40 lines each (to build).
- A task already shown in this session isn't shown again.

Next time anyone asks "set up the database" in Paytmcall:
- The rule "use neon, not local DB" is already in context.
- Recall shows task A with "user then corrected: use neon".

So the model never repeats the mistake.

## The second source: config and git (no talk needed)
Read fresh at every session start, so they never go stale:

| Fact | Read from |
|---|---|
| Package manager | lockfile (`pnpm-lock.yaml` → pnpm) |
| Test, lint, build commands | `package.json` scripts, `pyproject.toml` |
| Formatting | `.prettierrc`, ruff/black config |
| Strictness | `tsconfig.json` `strict` |
| Commit style | last 50 commit messages (e.g. `feat(scope): …`) |

These get source weight 1.0, so they're the most trusted facts. Some of them you'd never think to say out loud.

## Guarding against bad memory
| Risk | Guard |
|---|---|
| Wrong rule repeated every session | Inject only with evidence; `footprint memory list / forget <id>` to fix it by hand |
| Old decision, project moved on | Newer contradiction supersedes it; recency decay |
| Paytmcall rule leaks into footprint | Scope: a project rule only shows in its own project; user-wide needs 2+ projects |
| Context bloat | Fixed token budgets; ranked cut-off |
| Secrets | Redacted before anything is indexed |
| Bench answers leaking into memory | Held-out bench sessions are excluded (already built) |

## Built vs to build
| Part | Status |
|---|---|
| Segment, task history, BM25 recall, handover, redaction, bench holdout | **Built** (`main`) |
| Correction labeller, "user then corrected" in recall | Prototype (unmerged branch) |
| Archive, config/git profile, `rules.json` with scoring/merge/supersede, `AGENTS.md` block, own-diff examples, `memory list/forget` | **To build** |

## Still open
- **Merging by shared words** misses paraphrases ("use neon" vs "switch to serverless postgres"). Fix it only if the rule-precision check shows duplicates; embeddings would be the upgrade.
- **Wording:** keeping your exact words is safe but sometimes unclear. A local model could tidy them later, behind the same precision check.

Section 6 of the Notion plan has the schema and tiers, but not this step-by-step flow, the scoring formula, the config sources, the token budgets or the guards. Should I add them?

Here are five points to raise with your manager. Each comes with real numbers from your history, so it shows you've looked at the data.

**1. Memory keeps only facts backed by evidence, not everything that was said.**
Of 747 past prompts:
- 61% are one-off instructions
- 26% are questions
- 7% are pasted logs and specs
- 3% are acknowledgements ("ok, do it")

Only the 3% that are corrections, like "why are we using local DB, use neon", become rules. A rule needs evidence: a correction, repo config or git, or the same point in 2+ sessions. That's how we keep the data small without losing what matters.

**2. Users show their preferences by correcting, not by stating them.**
We tested extracting "always/never" statements from prompts and got zero real ones that recur. The real signal is pushback, plus what's already in the repo (lockfile, formatter config, test scripts, commit style). So the design reads behaviour and config instead of trusting what people say about themselves.

**3. Every rule is scored, scoped and can be superseded, so memory doesn't rot.**
- **Score:** source × repetition × recency. Config counts most, then corrections; a rule fades without fresh evidence.
- **Scope:** rules are per project, so a Paytmcall decision never leaks into another repo.
- **Superseded:** a newer contradiction replaces the old rule. The old one is kept for history but no longer used.

content.text:
"BM25 recall" combines two things: **BM25** is the search method, and **recall** is footprint's feature (`footprint recall`) that pulls up your similar past work. Note that "recall" here is just the feature's name, not the search-quality metric of the same name.

## BM25, simply
It's a keyword-search scoring method, the same family that classic search engines use. For a new prompt it scores each past task by:
1. **Shared words:** more matching words means a higher score.
2. **Rare words count more:** "neon" or "recording" matching is worth far more than "fix" or "add", which appear everywhere.
3. **Length fairness:** a long task doesn't win just because it has more words.

No AI model and no embeddings are involved. It's pure maths over word counts, so it's fast, free, runs offline, and gives the same result every time.

## How footprint uses it (already built, `memory.py`)
On every prompt you type:
1. It drops filler words ("the", "please", "fix", "add"…).
2. It scores all past tasks: your prompt and file names count most, and how the task ended counts a little.
3. Tasks from the **same project** get a 1.5× boost.
4. It keeps a task only if:
   - the score is at least 4,
   - it shares at least 2 meaningful words with your prompt,
   - and it's within half of the best match.
5. It takes the **top 3** at most, skipping any already shown in this session.
6. It adds them to your prompt (up to about 1500 characters) as "Similar past work": what you asked, the files, the commands, how it ended, and what you corrected.

You've seen it at work: those "Similar past work" blocks at the top of your messages in this chat come from it.

## Its weakness
It matches **words, not meaning**. "Use Neon" and "switch to serverless Postgres" share no words, so it misses the link. The fix is **semantic search** (embeddings), which matches meaning. The plan adds that only once a test shows BM25 missing relevant tasks, because BM25 is cheaper and often good enough.

result: BM25 recall is footprint's keyword search over your past tasks (rare words count more, same-project tasks boosted, top 3 kept) that adds "Similar past work" to each prompt; it matches words, not meaning, so semantic search is the later upgrade.

content.text:
Redaction means **finding secrets in text and replacing them with `[redacted]`** before the text is stored or used anywhere.

## Example
Before:
```
export [redacted]
[redacted]
```
After:
```
export [redacted]
[redacted]
```

## What footprint catches (`memory.py`, the `SECRET` pattern)
- **API keys by their shape:** OpenAI `sk-…`, GitHub `ghp_…` / `github_pat_…`, AWS `AKIA…`, Slack `xox…`, footprint `fp_…`, and JWT tokens `eyJ…`.
- **"name = value" settings:** `[redacted] `[redacted] `[redacted] `[redacted]
- **Environment variables with risky names:** `*_SECRET`, `*_TOKEN`, `*_PASSWORD`, `*_KEY`, `DATABASE_URL`, `DSN`…
- **Passwords inside URLs:** `user:password@host`.

## Why it matters here
Your chats contain real keys: you paste `.env` files, and commands print tokens. Anything footprint stores could otherwise leak into:
- the memory index,
- the prompts sent to cloud models like Big Pickle or GLM,
- the LoRA training data,
- or your GitHub vault through `sync`.

## Where it runs today
| Place | Redacted? |
|---|---|
| Memory index / recall | Yes (on `main`) |
| LoRA training data (`collect`) | **No on `main`.** 484 of 3942 examples matched. Yes on the prototype branch, where it dropped to 0. |

## Its limit
It works by **pattern matching**, so a secret with an unusual shape (say, a random password in plain text) can slip through. That's why the plan redacts **before** anything else reads the data, and keeps training data off GitHub by default.

result: Redaction replaces secrets (API keys, tokens, passwords, database URLs) with `[redacted]` before text is stored or sent; on `main` it covers memory but not training data (484 of 3942 examples matched), which the plan fixes first.

content.text:
Redaction matters to footprint specifically because **footprint takes your private chats and moves them to places they were never meant to go**. Without redaction, every one of those moves can leak a key.

## Where your secrets would travel without it

| Footprint feature | Where the text goes | Risk without redaction |
|---|---|---|
| **Recall / handover** | Into prompts sent to **cloud models** (Big Pickle, GLM, Gemini) | Your Neon password or API key is sent to a third party; free tiers may log or train on it. |
| **LoRA training** | Into the **model's weights** | The model can memorise a key and print it later in an answer. Weights can't be "un-learned"; you'd have to retrain. |
| **`sync push`** | To your **GitHub vault repo** | Keys sit in git history permanently, even after deletion. |
| **Product for other users** | Every user's laptop | One leak and nobody trusts footprint with their sessions. |

## It's not hypothetical
- Your current training file has **484 of 3942 examples** matching secret patterns.
- Your sessions often include commands like `set -a && source .env` and pasted `.env` contents.
- The "Similar past work" blocks in this chat get injected into prompts. They're safe only because recall redacts first.

## In one line
Footprint's whole job is **reusing your chats elsewhere**: other models, training, sync. Redaction is what makes that reuse safe. That's why it's phase 1 in the plan, before any personalisation work.

result: Redaction matters because footprint reuses your chats in cloud-model prompts, LoRA weights and the GitHub vault; without it your keys (484 of 3942 training examples match secret patterns) would leak to all three.

content.text:
Not quite: not many pipelines. Footprint has **one write pipeline** that builds memory, plus **two read paths** that use it. Fewer moving parts means fewer ways to break.

```
                    WRITE (builds memory)
sessions ──► archive ─► redact ─► segment ─► classify ─► extract ─► merge ─► score ─► store
                                                 │
                                                 └─► training data (same labels, separate output)

repo config + git ──► profile reader ─────────────────────────────────────────────► store
                       (small, runs fresh at each session start)

                    READ (uses memory)
session start ──► rules + profile + handover   (~1200 tokens)  ─► model
every prompt  ──► BM25 recall top 3 + your diffs (~800 tokens) ─► model
```

| Part | Runs when | Exists? |
|---|---|---|
| **Write pipeline** | After each session changes (incremental; only new or changed sessions are re-read) | Partly: segment, redact and the index are built; classify, extract, merge, score and rules are to build |
| **Profile reader** | Every session start (cheap: reads a few files and git log) | To build |
| **Session-start read** | When you open a session | Handover built; rules + `AGENTS.md` to build |
| **Per-prompt read** | Every prompt | BM25 recall built; own-diff examples to build |

## Why one write pipeline, not many
- **Redact once, at the front:** nothing downstream can see a secret.
- **Label once:** the same accepted/rejected label feeds both memory and training, so the two can never disagree.
- **Less to maintain:** each stage is a plain function in the same flow, with no separate services, queues or databases.

The profile reader stays separate because it reads **config files, not chats**. It needs nothing from the session pipeline.

result: Memory is one write pipeline (archive, redact, segment, classify, extract, merge, score, store) that also feeds training data, plus a small config/git profile reader and two read paths (session start and every prompt).

content.text:
No. Segment, BM25 and the rest are **stages (steps) inside one pipeline**, not separate pipelines. Each stage is one function: it takes the previous stage's output, does one job, and passes the result on, like an assembly line.

## Write side (builds memory), stage by stage

| # | Stage | Job | In → Out | Built? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Archive | Keep a copy before Claude Code deletes it | session file → archived copy | To build |
| 2 | Redact | Strip secrets | raw text → safe text | Built (memory) |
| 3 | Segment | Split the session into tasks | session → tasks (prompt + files + cmds + outcome) | Built |
| 4 | Classify | Label each message | message → correction / instruction / question / paste / acknowledgement | Prototype |
| 5 | Label tasks | Mark each task accepted or rejected | task + next message → label | Prototype |
| 6 | Extract | Pull candidate rules | corrections + config → candidate rules | To build |
| 7 | Merge | Join duplicates, supersede old rules | candidates + existing rules → updated rules | To build |
| 8 | Score | Rank by source × repetition × recency | rules → scored rules | To build |
| 9 | Store | Save to disk | → `memory.json` (tasks), `rules.json` (rules) | Tasks built, rules to build |

## Read side (uses memory), stage by stage

| # | Stage | Job | Built? |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1 | Filter | Keep only this project's items plus user-wide ones | Built (project boost) |
| R2 | **BM25 search** | Rank past tasks by word match with your prompt | Built |
| R3 | Pick | Top 3 above the threshold, skipping ones already shown | Built |
| R4 | Build context | Format rules + tasks + examples within the token budget | Partly built |
| R5 | Inject | Add to the session start or to your prompt | Built (hooks + OpenCode plugin) |

## Where BM25 sits
BM25 is on the **read side**, not the write side. The write side only stores tasks; BM25 searches them at the moment you type a prompt. That's why it needs no pre-built index: it scores about 750 tasks in milliseconds each time.

## Why stages instead of separate pipelines
- **One order, always the same:** redact always comes before anything reads the data.
- **Each stage is testable alone:** for example, the classifier already has its own test.
- **Easy to swap:** BM25 can later become BM25 + embeddings by changing stage R2 only; nothing else moves.

result: Segment, BM25 and the rest are stages in one assembly line, not separate pipelines: 9 write stages (archive through store) build memory, and 5 read stages (filter, BM25 search, pick, build context, inject) use it.

Source weight 1.0, the most trusted facts. | Fact | Read from | | --- | --- | | Package manager | Lockfile (`pnpm-lock.yaml` → pnpm) | | Test, lint, build commands | `package.json` scripts, `pyproject.toml` | | Formatting | `.prettierrc`, ruff or black config | | Strictness | `tsconfig.json` `strict` | | Commit style | Last 50 commit messages | ### Storage ``` ~/.footprint/archive/ raw sessions, redacted (never injected) ~/.footprint/memory.json task history index (exists today) ~/.footprint/rules.json promoted rules, schema v1 (to build) /AGENTS.md generated block of this project's rules, between markers (opt-in, later) ``` ### Token budgets | When | What | Budget | | --- | --- | --- | | Session start | Rules + profile, highest score first, this project plus user-wide | ~400 tokens | | Session start | Handover (last session's state) | ~800 tokens | | Every prompt | Top 3 similar past tasks with "user then corrected" + 1–2 of your own diffs (~40 lines each) | ~800 tokens | ### Guards against bad memory | Risk | Guard | | --- | --- | | Wrong rule repeated every session | Inject only with evidence; `footprint memory list / forget ` to remove it | | Old decision, project moved on | Newer contradiction supersedes it; recency decay | | One project's rule leaks into another | Scope: project rules show only in their project; user-wide needs 2+ projects | | Context bloat | Fixed token budgets; ranked cut-off | | Secrets | Redacted before anything is indexed | | Bench answers leaking into memory | Held-out bench sessions excluded (built) | | Paraphrases not merged ("use neon" vs "switch to serverless postgres") | Accept for now; add embeddings only if the precision check shows duplicates | ### Memory build plan Nothing technical blocks this. Memory does not depend on the hardware, model or LoRA decisions. **Settle before building:** | Item | Why it matters | Default | | --- | --- | --- | | Build on the prototype branch | Labeller and training redaction already exist on `worktree-distill-pipeline`; `main` lacks them | Yes: continue there, then merge | | Write `AGENTS.md` into repos | Changes files inside your projects | Off at first; hooks only; opt-in later | | Stop Claude Code deleting old sessions | Edits `~/.claude/settings.json` (`cleanupPeriodDays`) | Yes, with your approval of the edit | | Small bench (1 task) | Blocks proving memory helps (B beats A), not building it | Grow the bench alongside | **Build order, each step tested before the next:** 1. Archive: copy all existing and new sessions, redacted. 2. Classifier and labels: merge the prototype; add question, paste and acknowledgement types. 3. Profile reader: lockfile, formatter, test command, commit style. 4. Rules store: extract from corrections, merge, supersede, score → `rules.json`. 5. Injection: rules and profile at session start, within the token budget. 6. `footprint memory list / forget`: remove a wrong rule by hand. 7. Check: rule precision on your data (you mark each listed rule right or wrong) and a correction-rate baseline. Real runs use your data in a temp folder, so live memory is untouched until merge.
